title: nuSTORM: a unique GeV electron-(anti)neutrino machine
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, proceedings at Ultra-Cold Muons for the LHC Workshop, September 2026
summary: In this conference contribution, I briefly review current experimental programmes measuring the Dirac CP phase δCP using accelerator neutrinos. I argue that the nuSTORM concept---neutrino beams from a muon storage ring---could provide high-quality electron-(anti)neutrino beams needed for the cross-section inputs to δCP measurements.

title: Heat cleaning kinetics and thermal degradation of MOCVD-grown GaAs photocathodes
summary: We evaluated metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD)-grown GaAs/GaAsP strained-superlattice photocathodes with integrated distributed Bragg reflectors in a low-voltage Mott polarimeter at Jefferson Lab. Without a protective arsenic cap, surface contamination can develop during transport and installation. Heat cleaning removes this contamination by thermally desorbing material bound to the surface, but excessive heating can also damage the photocathode. We modeled quantum efficiency (QE) in terms of surface contaminant coverage to describe its increase with heating time. QE rose more rapidly and reached a plateau nearly twice as high at $550^\circ\text{C}$ as at $450^\circ\text{C}$, while polarization remained near 83%. Further heating reduced QE and polarization. Reflectance measurements showed a shift of the optical resonance to shorter wavelengths, consistent with surface material loss. We also tested the cleaning method in a high-voltage photogun, where QE showed the same initial increase and subsequent decline. The cleaning procedure must therefore balance contaminant removal against loss of photocathode material.

title: Feasibility study of two-stage direct laser acceleration of electrons
summary: We present the first numerical demonstration of two-stage direct laser acceleration (DLA) of electrons. The result was obtained using quasi-3D particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. The first stage ($a_0 = 6$, $τ= 200~\mathrm{fs}$, $w = 4λ$, $λ= 0.8~μ\mathrm{m}$) utilized a nitrogen gas target with an atomic density of $n_a = 0.008n_{cr}$. This stage was designed to accelerate low-energy electrons, achieving a maximum energy of approximately 94 MeV with a two-temperature energy spectrum ($T_1 = 7.0$ MeV and $T_2 = 16.0$ MeV) and a charge of 6.04 nC ($\mathcal{E} > 5$ MeV). The resulting electron bunch was then injected into the second stage, where hydrogen at a lower density ($n_a = 0.01n_{cr}$) was used, while the laser parameters were the same as in the first stage except that the waist was increased to $w = 8λ$. After the second stage, the electrons reached energies up to 225 MeV, with a two-temperature energy spectrum ($T_1 = 18.4$ MeV and $T_2 = 88.3$ MeV) and a charge of 4.55 nC ($\mathcal{E} > 5$ MeV). The self-injected electrons in the second stage reached a maximum energy of 123 MeV with a charge of 1.14 nC ($\mathcal{E} > 5$ MeV). The simulation results are compared with a theoretical DLA model, which describes the electron motion in the combined fields of the laser pulse and the quasistatic plasma channel. The model accounts for the transverse size of the channel by incorporating a Gaussian attenuation of the channel fields and off-axis injection. The theoretical model correctly describes the observed acceleration dynamics for both low-energy and pre-accelerated electrons, confirming its validity for designing multi-stage DLA schemes. Thus, the implementation of multi-stage acceleration by the DLA mechanism is successfully demonstrated for the first time in a numerical experiment.

title: A conservative latent neural ODE for stiff collisional-radiative plasma kinetics
summary: Collisional-radiative (CR) models govern the non equilibrium population kinetics of partially ionized plasmas and are a dominant cost in integrated edge and divertor plasma simulations, where a stiff system of dozens to thousands of coupled rate equations must be solved at every spatial cell and time step. We present a two-stage machine learning (ML) surrogate that replaces the direct CR solve with a compact, continuous-time, deployable dynamical model. Stage~1 is a grey-box autoencoder that compresses a high-dimensional ion population vector into a low-dimensional latent space in which four coordinates, one per charge state of the lithium system studied here, are \emph{fixed} to the physical charge-state distribution and the rest are learned. Stage~2 is a latent neural ODE that learns the continuous-time evolution of the latent variables. We (i) integrate in a density-folded, logarithmic clock on which the latent trajectory is smooth enough for an explicit integrator, (ii) sample time adaptively by latent arc length so the sharp ionization transition is resolved, (iii) add a linear damping toward an estimate of the CR steady state as a design choice, and (iv) enforce mass conservation directly. The surrogate is accurate, with a charge-state error that is unchanged under refinement of its output grid, over full-trajectory rollouts within the trained horizon, and exactly conservative: on $1480$ held-out trajectories at the trained conditions it reproduces the charge-state evolution with a median absolute error of $4.2\times10^{-3}$ on fractions in $[0,1]$, conserves mass to $10^{-7}$, {and evaluates a full sixteen-decade trajectory in ${\sim}76\,μ$s per trajectory in batched inference on a single GPU.} A model retrained with whole $(\nA,\Te)$ grid points withheld is equally accurate at those unseen conditions.

title: Measuring and predicting plasma blob influence on downstream transport through paired simulations
summary: We use two-dimensional TOKAM2D simulations of flux-driven turbulence to measure how much a single plasma blob affects particle transport farther out in the scrape-off layer. We evolve the same turbulent state twice, weakening the density and potential variations of one blob in one of the two simulations. The resulting difference in outward particle flux, integrated over time in each poloidal sector of a downstream band, defines the blob's influence vector $α$. Its magnitude falls steeply with distance from the band and generally increases with blob size and density content. Even blobs with similar bulk properties can differ in influence by orders of magnitude. A graph neural network that uses the recent evolution of the fields in and around each blob predicts much of this difference for pairs of otherwise similar blobs. To see how the difference develops, we compare the downstream density and radial velocity in the two simulations. For both strongly and weakly influential blobs in the pairs examined, changes in radial velocity account for most of the local change in outward flux. In the stronger responses, the density and flow contributions tend to reinforce each other in the same sectors at the same times.

title: Learning effective stochastic predator and prey dynamics across physical and biological systems from limited data
summary: Constructing an effective low-dimensional stochastic model from sparse observations requires separating deterministic drift from state-dependent fluctuations when the governing interaction law is unknown. We formulate an adaptive neural stochastic differential equation with topology constraints (TC-AdaNSDE) for two-variable predator--prey dynamics. To regularize the inverse problem when data are scarce, the model combines flexible drift and correlated diffusion fields with density-adaptive local Kramers--Moyal moment estimates and soft phase-space constraints reflecting boundary saddle behavior near extinction and local stability near coexistence. Using a known nonlinear stochastic system, we first show that short-time trajectory error cannot assess diffusion accuracy on its own and must be paired with distributional measures of one-step transitions and long-time phase-space occupancy. We then apply this framework to macroscopic turbulence and zonal flow energies reduced from Hasegawa--Wakatani plasma simulations and to short ecological time series. In the sparse-data regime, TC-AdaNSDE reproduces both short-horizon evolution and long-time invariant energy distributions where deterministic reductions collapse and unconstrained stochastic fits diverge, while recovering physically interpretable drift and fluctuation fields across both physical and biological systems.

title: Edge transport mechanisms in small-ELM and type-I ELM regimes at JET using global gyrokinetic simulations
summary: To explore tokamak operating regimes that combine high energy confinement with edge dynamics relevant for ITER, new regimes with small edge-localized modes (ELMs), referred to as baseline small-ELM (BSE), have been obtained at JET with the Be wall and W divertor. In this work, the edge transport mechanisms in a selected BSE discharge are compared with those in a standard H-mode with type-I ELMs using radially global gyrokinetic simulations with the GENE code. The simulations use experimental input profiles and include kinetic electrons and deuterium ions, electromagnetic (EM) effects, and the radially varying equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. At low toroidal mode number $n$, the type-I ELM pedestal is found to be unstable to kinetic-ballooning modes (KBMs), with radial mode structures covering the full pedestal. In the BSE regime, no KBM branch is found, and the same spectral range is dominated by hybrid ITG--TEM modes. The modifications of the linear modes by finite$-β$ effects are discussed in details. In nonlinear simulations of the type-I ELM regime, KBM-driven turbulence produces high transport levels that are resilient to the equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. By contrast, in the BSE regime, EM effects moderately increase transport, which is strongly regulated by the equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. The two regimes also differ in their radial turbulence organization and in the amplitude and persistence of the zonal shearing rate. These results identify the interplay between EM effects and equilibrium $E\times B$ flow as a key element of edge transport regulation.

title: Hot-Layer Ignition in High-Gain Inertial Confinement Fusion
summary: Ignition of the shocked deuterium tritium shell is identified during the thermonuclear combustion of very high-gain targets in inertial confinement fusion (ICF). This mechanism is due to the local energy deposition of the fusion alphas created in this shocked shell, independently of hot-spot ignition, and generates sufficient energy to fully recompress the hot spot. A new analytical criterion for the ignition of the hot layer is presented. A simple three zone model, based on the thick layer hot-spot model, reproduces this mechanism, which breaks down into successive stages: ignition of the hot spot, compression of the shocked shell, ignition of the shocked shell, and subsequent recompression of the hot spot. 1D numerical simulations highlight the onset of this hot layer ignition thereby satisfying the analytical ignition criterion. It is shown that this mechanism amplifies the energy released by the combustion of the target by approximately 50 %.
